issues.explanation: For a combat trauma profile, 'kids crying' is not impossible, but it is a relatively specific trigger that would usually be supported by memory or appraisal content involving civilians/children; here the memory and appraisal items do not provide that link, so this trigger is hard to integrate with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: 'My body has been permanently damaged by what happened' implies an enduring physical injury theme, but the rest of the selected items do not support a bodily injury-focused combat presentation: memory items emphasize fragmentation/unreality, triggers emphasize intrusion/power imbalance, and strategies emphasize avoidance/hypervigilance rather than injury management. This appraisal is insufficiently anchored in the rest of the profile.

vignette: Marika, a 66-year-old curriculum designer from the South Island, recalls a night in Afghanistan when a sudden burst of fire and a distant roar of a helicopter cut across the darkness, turning her world into a flash of shattered glass and a relentless thud of metal overhead. The sound of that helicopter, even years later, still erupts in her mind like a jarring flash, pulling the memory of that night into her present awareness. Each time the engine whirrs, she is suddenly flooded with the image of a white-armored vehicle, a squad of soldiers, and the oppressive weight of a commander's orders that left her unable to decide. This auditory trigger not only summons the memory but also stirs a sharp awareness of power imbalance, reminding her of how men in uniforms had taken command of her life and of the feeling that she was merely a spectator. The memory itself is fragmented, each piece arriving like a disjointed shard that she cannot string together; the story feels unreal, and when she attempts to describe it, words fail her, adding to her sense of confusion. These fragments, when triggered by a sudden sound or a scene that resembles a battlefield, become triggers in and of themselves, perpetuating the cycle of intrusion. Because she can't trust that she will do the right thing, she feels intense self-doubt, and because she constantly senses that others hold power over her, she becomes isolated and hyper-vigilant, always on guard for the next command that might come. This negative appraisal of herself and the world pushes her toward maladaptive strategies: she deliberately avoids going outside, staying close to an exit, and shuns any emotional swell, believing that feeling too much would render her vulnerable. The very avoidance that keeps her safe in the moment reinforces her self-doubt, as she sees herself as someone who cannot be relied upon in a crisis, and her isolation grows as she keeps her distance from coworkers and friends, believing they cannot help or understand her. By staying near the exit, she also turns the exit itself into a trigger-when she hears the click of a door or the hiss of a hallway's air conditioning, she is reminded of the moment she saw a bunker's doorway and felt the oppressive presence of authority. This constant vigilance, born from the same appraisal that fuels her avoidance, sharpens her sensitivity to any hint of power imbalance, making ordinary meetings feel like a threat and encouraging her to remain on the periphery. When she finally sits in the corner of the classroom design studio and refuses to feel the rising anxiety, the memory remains stuck in those fragmented, disjointed pieces, never processed or integrated. Each avoidance of feeling, each attempt to stay near an exit, and each avoidance of stepping outside, in turn, feeds back into the memory and the negative appraisal, leaving her in a loop that has become increasingly hard to break. After months of this cycle, her productivity declined; the detailed curriculum plans she once loved became rushed, and her colleagues noticed her withdrawal, which further deepened her isolation. The culmination of these experiences-an ever-present sense that she is alone, that she cannot trust herself to make the right decision, and that any sudden sound or movement might bring her back to that night-finally pushed her to seek help. Marika now hopes that by sharing her story, she might regain control over the intrusive memories and the overwhelming sense of powerlessness that have defined her life for decades, while fearing that if she cannot break this cycle, she will remain forever trapped in the echo of that distant helicopter.
